candidates: In mermaid diagram modules, follow the established file naming convention: files containing diagram data/state must be named `*Db.ts` (e.g., `classDb.ts`), and files containing Jison grammar belong in the `parser/` subdirectory or are named accordingly. Do not name a data/state file `*Parser` — `Parser` is reserved for grammar files.

In `parseGenericTypes` (and any string-replacement loop in `packages/mermaid/src/diagrams/common/common.ts`), never use a recursive call to re-run the replacement. If the regex fails to make progress on a given input, recursion will never reach a base case and will throw `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`. Use an iterative `do…while` loop with a convergence check instead.

When modifying the tilde-based generic type parsing (e.g., `~T~` syntax in class diagrams), add explicit test cases for: (1) multiple generic parameters in a single method signature (e.g., `getTimes(List~T~, List~OT~)`), (2) composite generics (e.g., `List~K, V~`), and (3) nested generics (e.g., `List~List~T~~`). Symmetric delimiters like `~` are inherently ambiguous for multiple-parameter generics; document the known limitation or support an asymmetric alternative such as `<>` via HTML-escaping.

In Cypress/Vitest snapshot tests, do not manually number test description strings (e.g., avoid prefixes like `17a:`, `18b:`). New tests should use plain descriptive names. When the same assertion applies to multiple similar values, prefer a parameterized pattern (`describe` + `for` loop) rather than copy-pasting numbered test cases. Renaming existing numbered tests should be done in a separate dedicated PR to avoid invalidating Applitools visual baseline snapshots.

When a pull request mixes cosmetic changes (removing redundant comments, reformatting) with functional changes, put the cosmetic work in a separate, clearly labelled git commit (e.g., `chore: remove redundant inline comments`). This makes the functional diff significantly easier to review.

Add TSDoc comments to all newly exported TypeScript classes and their public properties/methods. At a minimum, provide a one-sentence class-level description and clarify any field whose meaning is not obvious from its name alone (e.g., distinguish a DOM-unique id from a diagram-scoped id). This allows editors to surface documentation inline when a consumer is using the class.

Prefer template literals over string concatenation in TypeScript source files (e.g., use `` `(${parseGenericTypes(this.parameters.trim())})` `` rather than `'(' + parseGenericTypes(this.parameters.trim()) + ')'`). The project may enforce this via the `prefer-template` ESLint rule.

Do not remove comments that explain *why* a non-obvious implementation choice was made, even if the comment seems redundant at first glance. For example, a comment explaining why `.replace()` is called in a loop instead of `.replaceAll()` guards against a future 'simplification' that would reintroduce a bug. Only remove comments that literally restate what the code already says.

Mark TypeScript class methods that are only intended for internal use as `private`. This shrinks the public API surface, prevents callers from depending on implementation details, and makes the intended access pattern explicit without requiring runtime enforcement.

Use TypeScript union types instead of plain `string` for any field or parameter that accepts only a fixed set of values (e.g., `memberType: 'method' | 'attribute'` and `visibility: '#' | '+' | '~' | '-' | ''`). This catches invalid values at compile time and documents the valid set directly in the type signature.

Within a diagram-specific module (e.g., any file under `src/diagrams/class/`), do not prefix exported names with the diagram type name. The module path already provides that context. Follow the existing convention: export `Renderer`, `Parser`, `Styles` rather than `ClassRenderer`, `ClassParser`, `ClassStyles`.

When refactoring to move functionality into a new class, ensure that input sanitization previously performed by the caller is migrated into the new class's constructor. A class that accepts user-supplied strings must call `sanitizeText` (or equivalent) before storing them, rather than relying on callers to pre-sanitize.

When multiple properties of a method's return value are needed in the same scope, call the method exactly once and destructure the result into named variables (e.g., `const { displayText, cssStyle } = member.getDisplayDetails();`). Avoid calling the same method multiple times in the same function to retrieve different properties — it is redundant and fragile if the method has any side effects or cost.

Changes to Jison grammar rules or parsing logic in mermaid diagram parsers must not break backward compatibility with existing valid diagram syntax. Before removing or altering a grammar rule, verify that all previously supported syntax still renders correctly. Add regression tests for any syntax that lacks existing coverage.
